title: Sentiment
subtitle: Type a company to get a read

bigPicture.lead: Funding AI is the story across big tech this week.
body: Each read covers the last 3 to 5 days and starts from whatever moved the stock: earnings, an equity raise, a regulatory step, or a deal debate.
This week the market rewarded companies that fund AI from their own cash (Microsoft) and punished cash burn or new equity (Alphabet, Amazon, Meta).

driver.title: Search growth slowed to 12% as AI Mode earns less per query

tickers.verdict: Bearish: Search revenue growth slowed sharply and the market repriced Search, even with Cloud doubling.
tickers.topTheme: Search slowing, AI Mode monetizes less
tickers.changed: Reframed around the real driver: the Search growth slowdown. Move confirmed at about 12.6% on Oct 29.

overview.lean: Bearish near term, constructive on 12 months among the Street.

camps.name: Search bears
camps.argues: AI Mode answers more questions but carries fewer ads, so Search growth falling from 17% to 12% is structural, not a blip.

camps.name: Long-term bulls
camps.argues: AI Mode queries are longer and Cloud grew over 100%, so monetization catches up and the selloff overshoots.

overview.agree: Nearly everyone agrees the problem is Search monetization, not Cloud. Cloud more than doubled.
overview.split: Split on whether lower revenue per search is temporary (ads still being added inside AI Mode) or permanent.

shift.note: After the close, the headline miss and negative free cash flow drew immediate selling.
Down about 13% intraday, on track for its worst post-earnings day on record. The Search slowdown became the single story.
Bull rebuttals and dip buying appear, but the high-reach framing is still Search repricing.

overview.hinges: Whether Google can put enough ads into AI Mode to lift revenue per query back up.

tickers.whatHappened: Alphabet reported Q3 on Oct 28. Search revenue grew 12% to $63.35B (Oct 28), down from 17% in Q2, while Cloud grew 103% to $30.7B (Oct 28) and free cash flow was negative $9.07B (Oct 28). Management said AI Mode queries carry lower monetization. The stock fell about 12.6% on Oct 29, its worst post-earnings day on record, erasing roughly $500B of value.
tickers.howReading: Credible voices read it as a repricing of Search economics rather than a rejection of Google's AI position: more questions, less money per question. A minority, including former fund manager Rahul Sharma, point out paid clicks still grew 8% and cost per click 4%, so the slowdown is fewer monetized clicks, not price. The Street mostly cut targets but kept ratings.

driver.title: Azure grew 48% and was guided to 49% to 50%, while staying cash positive

tickers.move: +4% after hours Oct 28, roughly flat Oct 29

camps.argues: Azure accelerated to 48% with a 49% to 50% guide and positive free cash flow, unlike peers.

camps.argues: Lower capex reflects late third-party capacity, not discipline, so spend catches up later.

overview.agree: Agree Microsoft had the best AI funding story of the week.

Gains faded to roughly flat as the Alphabet selloff hit the group.

tickers.whatHappened: Microsoft reported fiscal Q1 on Oct 28. Revenue was $92.3B vs $90.7B expected (Oct 28) and Azure grew 48% to $33.2B (Oct 28), with next quarter guided to 49% to 50% against about 44.6% expected. Capex of $45.2B came in under estimates and calendar 2026 capex was trimmed to about $170B because third-party capacity arrived late. Free cash flow fell 27% but stayed positive at $18.6B.
tickers.howReading: High-signal accounts framed Microsoft as the self-funding AI winner against Alphabet, Meta and Amazon, which all burned cash. The CFO's line that demand still exceeds supply got the most pickup. The main reservation is that lower capex is timing rather than discipline.

driver.title: Up to $97.5B equity raise with nonvoting Class C shares, offset by Muse momentum

tickers.move: About -2% Oct 26, about -1% Oct 27, -1.2% to -1.4% Oct 29
tickers.verdict: Mixed: a record equity raise and dilution weigh on the stock, offset by Muse momentum and Nvidia buying in.
tickers.topTheme: Equity raise and Class C vs Muse momentum
tickers.changed: Driver changed from Q3 earnings to the Oct 26 equity raise, with Muse momentum as the offset.

camps.name: Dilution and governance bears
camps.argues: Up to $97.5B of stock, nonvoting Class C shares and a pension fund lawsuit mean shareholders fund AI while Zuckerberg keeps control.

camps.name: Muse bulls
camps.argues: Muse is one of the fastest-growing consumer AI apps and Nvidia and AMD are investing $4B alongside, so the spend has a product.

overview.agree: Agree the raise is about funding AI capex after free cash flow turned negative.
overview.split: Split on whether Muse engagement is durable; one Sensor Tower based post says most users stopped returning after two weeks (low reach, unverified).

shift.note: Raise announced: $35B underwritten plus a $60B Class C at-the-market program. Stock down nearly 2%.
Upsized to $25B common at $625 plus $12.5B preferred. Nvidia commits $3B and expands the Muse partnership. Pension fund sues over the restructuring.
Offerings close; stock down about 1.2% on dilution worries.

overview.hinges: Whether Muse and AI revenue grow fast enough to justify roughly 5% to 6% dilution and the credit-market stress.

tickers.whatHappened: On Oct 26 Meta launched its largest-ever equity raise: $25B of Class A common priced at $625 via forward sales (no upfront cash, settles by Nov 19, 2027), $12.5B of 6.50% mandatory convertible preferred, and a planned $60B at-the-market program in new nonvoting Class C shares starting in Q1 2027. On Oct 27 Nvidia committed $3B and AMD $1B, and Nvidia expanded its partnership on Muse, Meta's AI agent. This followed Q3 results on Oct 21 with negative free cash flow of $2.12B and record 5-year CDS spreads.
tickers.howReading: Credible voices read it as Meta funding AI with shareholders' money while protecting Zuckerberg's control, which is why Barron's and a pension fund lawsuit focused on the Class C structure. Analysts estimate full execution could dilute holders by about 5% to 6% (Investing.com, Oct 29). The offset is Muse: Nvidia's investment and the expanded partnership are read as validation of demand. The credit angle (record CDS after Q3) keeps the debate in the bond market too.

tickers.verdict: Mixed: regulatory overhang from the DOJ, offset by expanding Meta demand.

overview.agree: Agree the DOJ step is an inquiry, not a lawsuit.
overview.split: Split on circular financing: Nvidia funding a top customer is read as validation by some and a red flag by others.

tickers.whatHappened: On Oct 28 Reuters reported the DOJ is asking whether Nvidia's $12.93B Hugging Face purchase would let it control a key distribution point for AI, as part of a broader conduct probe covering sales practices. Shares slipped 1% to 1.7% that day. A day earlier, Nvidia committed $3B to Meta's equity offering and Meta agreed to expand Vera Rubin deployment. Its last earnings were Aug 26; the next report date was just announced.
tickers.howReading: Headline accounts with the largest reach (Walter Bloomberg, Investing.com, WOLF) carried the DOJ story; analysis was limited. Credible voices treat it as an overhang rather than a thesis change, while the Meta investment revived circular-financing worries.

driver.title: Third quarter beat, but a fourth quarter guide far below the Street on a sharp PC slowdown

tickers.move: Down about 25% to 29% intraday on October 30 (around $66), after closing near $92 on October 29; on track for its worst day on record
tickers.verdict: Bearish: the PC reset and a cash-burning 2027 overwhelm a strong server quarter, and the Street is cutting targets across the board.
tickers.topTheme: PC collapse swamps the server CPU boom
tickers.changed: New read. First time Intel is tracked.

overview.lean: Bearish near term. Even the bulls concede the guide was a reset; the debate is whether the long-term foundry and server thesis survives it.

camps.name: Reset bears (most of the sell side)
camps.argues: The PC business hit a wall, Intel did not see it coming, its factories are still sized for PCs rather than servers, and 2027 is a heavy capex year with free cash flow probably not positive. BofA downgraded to neutral; Bernstein, UBS, Wells Fargo and Barclays cut targets to $75 to $80.

camps.name: Long-term bulls
camps.argues: Server CPU demand is extraordinary (Intel sees server CPU TAM growing up to 5x over five years, units up 30%+ in 2026 and 2027), data center grew 78%, and the foundry story did not change. Patrick Moorhead said the reaction does not make sense.

overview.agree: Agree the third quarter itself was good and that server demand is real but supply constrained (substrates, the Israel fab outage). Agree the PC slump runs at least through the first half of 2027 with no memory price relief.
overview.split: Split on whether a demand boom Intel cannot fully supply is a temporary bottleneck or proof it is losing the CPU cycle to AMD and TSMC.

shift.note: Intel announces the Classiq quantum software deal; read as a sign of balance sheet confidence. Stock near its best year on record.
Before the report the stock slips about 3.6%. After the bell, the Q4 guide of $15B to $16B against about $17B expected sends shares down more than 20% after hours.
Wave of target cuts and a BofA downgrade. Shares fall as much as 29%, and Intel's 5-year credit default swap widens to a record.

overview.hinges: Whether server supply (substrates, the Israel fab, shifting Oregon capacity to Intel 3) ramps through 2027 fast enough to offset PCs, and whether Intel names the external packaging and foundry customers it teased for the next two quarters.

tickers.whatHappened: On October 29 after the close, Intel reported third quarter revenue of $16.5B, up 21%, and adjusted EPS of $0.52 against $0.40 expected. Data center and AI revenue rose 78% to $7.3B, while client computing fell 5% to $8.1B. The fourth quarter guide was $15B to $16B in revenue and $0.25 adjusted EPS, against roughly $17B and $0.43 expected (LSEG). Management said the PC correction accelerated over the last two months, expects client revenue down more than 20% sequentially, sees the PC slowdown lasting at least through the first half of 2027, and said Intel does not expect positive cash flow this year. The October explosion at its Israel fab is expected to cost roughly $600M of revenue over two quarters (Reuters). On October 30 the stock fell as much as 29%, its sharpest one-day drop on record.
tickers.howReading: The sell side read it as a reset, not a blip. BofA's Vivek Arya downgraded to neutral and cut his target to $100 from $145, citing too little external foundry traction and a sharp PC drop. Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon cut to $75 from $110, modeling data center well above the Street but client far below it, with Intel shifting some Oregon capacity from PCs to server chips. UBS, Wells Fargo, Barclays and Goldman framed it as a PC hole that swallows the server upside. Industry analyst Patrick Moorhead is the main credible pushback: he called the quarter good, said the selloff does not make sense for a multiyear foundry thesis, and pointed to AMD's report next week as the test of whether the supply pain is Intel specific. The biggest reach on X was headline traffic (Walter Bloomberg, StockMKTNewz, Investing.com) on the record drop and record-wide credit spreads.

driver.title: Preliminary third quarter beat plus Brad Jacobs' separate $1B CKX Lands venture, with Jacobs staying QXO CEO

tickers.move: Up about 19% to 21% intraday on November 9 (about $13.73 to $13.94 around midday) from an $11.56 close on November 6. Earlier in the window: up 8.1% to $12.66 on November 4, down 8.1% to $11.64 on November 5, down 0.7% on November 6.
tickers.verdict: Mixed, leaning positive: a revenue beat and better pricing sparked a relief rally off depressed levels, but the stock is still less than half its 52-week high, the housing and roofing backdrop is weak, and Jacobs now splits time with a second $1B vehicle.
tickers.topTheme: Relief rally on a September beat, with a Jacobs side venture in the background
tickers.changed: New read. First time QXO is tracked.

overview.lean: Mixed, leaning positive. The tape voted bullish on November 9, but the sell side has been cutting targets for a month and almost nobody credible on X is making a strong call on QXO itself; attention went to the CKX deal.

camps.name: Execution bulls (sell side on Buy, Jacobs loyalists)
camps.argues: September came in much stronger than expected, roofing pricing turned positive (up 4.1% in September) and October daily roofing sales rose 9.1%, so QXO is gaining share in a weak market. Management targets about $4B of adjusted EBITDA by 2030, or up to about $5.5B with internally funded deals, and has more than $2B of liquidity with no maturities before 2031. All 12 tracked analysts rate it Buy (TipRanks).

camps.name: Macro and dilution skeptics
camps.argues: Growth is almost all acquired (Beacon, Kodiak, TopBuild), GAAP is still a loss of about $123M, residential roofing is in one of its weakest markets in years with no storm season, and targets have been cut hard since October (Truist to $15, Wells Fargo to $15, RBC to $18, Baird to $20, Citi to $22).

camps.name: Key-man worriers
camps.argues: Jacobs launching a ninth company through CKX Lands, with an undecided industry and its own $1B war chest, takes time and possibly future deals away from QXO. Jacobs answered on the call that he is 100% committed and owns about a quarter of QXO.

overview.agree: Agree the preliminary quarter was better than feared (revenue about $4.90B against roughly $4.83B to $4.85B expected) and that Jacobs staying as QXO chairman and CEO removed the worst reading of the CKX news. Agree CKX is Jacobs' personal vehicle, not a QXO deal.
overview.split: Split on whether one strong September and October means the cycle is turning or just a good month in a weak market, and on whether a second Jacobs roll-up vehicle helps QXO (proof he has built a team that can run without him) or hurts it (attention and deal-flow conflict).

shift.note: Stock up 8.1% to $12.66 on heavy call buying (MarketBeat) and integration optimism; no single company headline confirmed.

Down 8.1% to $11.64. Citi cut its target to $22 from $25 (Buy kept) on weaker residential and storm demand, the day after Owens Corning reported roofing revenue down 16% and called it one of the most challenging residential markets in years.

Before the open QXO pre-announces third quarter results and JPE announces the $1B CKX Lands investment. On the 8:30 AM Eastern call Jacobs says he is 100% committed to QXO. Stock up about 19% to 21% by midday.

overview.hinges: The full third quarter report and 10-Q on November 12 (margins, transaction costs, any fourth quarter color), whether the roofing price and October volume gains hold into winter, and whether Jacobs keeps QXO as the clear priority for building-products deals once CKX picks its industry.

tickers.whatHappened: On November 9 QXO pre-announced third quarter 2026 results: net sales of about $4.90B, up 79% from $2.73B, adjusted EBITDA of about $557M, up 85% from $301M (11.4% margin), and a GAAP net loss of about $123M against $139M a year earlier (QXO release). Growth was mostly from the Kodiak and TopBuild acquisitions. Jacobs said September came in much stronger than expected; roofing pricing went from down 1.1% in April to up 4.1% in September, and October daily roofing sales rose 9.1% (company total up 5.4%). Full results come November 12. The same morning, Jacobs Private Equity II (JPE, Jacobs' family office) and co-investors led by HRTG Partners (formerly Sequoia Heritage) agreed to invest $1B in cash in CKX Lands (NYSE American: CKX), a Louisiana land company with oil and gas royalties, timber and surface rents and a market value of about $21M. JPE puts in $900M and co-investors $100M, for voting convertible perpetual preferred convertible into about 219M shares at $4.57 (post a 4.174-for-1 reverse split; $1.09 pre-split) plus about 219M warrants struck at $4.57 (50%), $6.85 (25%) and $13.70 (25%). Investors would own about 99.78% on a fully converted basis before warrants. Existing CKX holders get a $20.8M special dividend ($10.1312 a share). Closing is expected in early 2027, subject to a CKX shareholder vote; holders of about 28% of the vote have signed support agreements. Jacobs becomes CKX chairman and CEO, the company will be renamed, and its industry is still to be determined. QXO itself is not an investor and puts in no money.
tickers.howReading: The sell side stayed constructive but cautious: every tracked analyst is at Buy, yet targets were cut through October and again by Citi on November 5, so the November 9 beat reads as relief rather than a re-rating. Coverage from The Motley Fool and Benzinga framed the rally as the revenue beat plus reassurance that Jacobs stays at QXO. On X, credible attention went almost entirely to the CKX deal: Bloomberg and Investing.com carried it as news, Investing.com called the size of a bet with no chosen industry the real story, and FreightWaves' John Kingston asked what Jacobs will do with $1B in a $21M company. Smaller accounts split between seeing it as a distraction for QXO and as a sign QXO is set up well enough to run without his full attention. High-reach posts about QXO itself were scarce in the window; the cashtag was dominated by spam and WhatsApp-group promos, which were excluded.

driver.title: First investor day in nine years: Full Stride Ahead strategy and 2031 financial framework

tickers.move: On November 17 the stock popped in premarket, with The Fly printing about $40.80, up about 7% from the November 16 close of $38.26. It opened at $40.20, traded as high as $40.67, then faded through the morning. As of 11:41 AM Central it was $37.50, down $0.76 or 2.0%, with a session low of $37.17 (Yahoo Finance, 12:41 PM Eastern, market still open). Around 10:50 AM Central, as the webcast continued, The Fly had it down about 1% at $38.05.
tickers.verdict: Mixed, leaning cautious: long-term margin and EPS targets came in above Street models and sparked a premarket pop, but the stock gave that back as investors focused on a back-weighted plan that does not restore growth until fiscal 2029 and barely rebuilds sales to fiscal 2026 levels.
tickers.topTheme: A premarket pop on 2031 margin targets faded once the wait for growth and the modest sales math sank in
tickers.changed: New read. First time NKE is tracked. Coverage is still partial: the public webcast runs until about 12:00 PM Pacific (2:00 PM Central), and Q&A had not been fully reported when this was written.

overview.lean: Mixed, leaning cautious. The first reaction to the 2031 margin and EPS targets was bullish, but by late morning the tape had reversed and the sell side was split between calling the framework a conservative floor and calling it aggressive and too far out.

camps.name: Floor bulls (Jefferies, and to a degree Baird)
camps.argues: Jefferies analyst Randal Konik (Buy) called the 2031 framework 'the credible floor we hoped for,' saying the $5B of incremental sales off the fiscal 2027 trough looks beatable and that waiting until fiscal 2029 for market-level growth gives innovation time to scale (WWD). Baird's Jonathan Komp called it a constructive step toward rebuilding confidence, said the timeline looks reasonable given a pipeline that should gain traction from late 2027 into 2028, and still wants proof of successful launches and a better marketplace, especially in Greater China (Investing.com).

camps.name: Margin-recovery realists (Stifel Hold, RBC Sector Perform)
camps.argues: The equity story is the margin rebuild, not a big sales rebound. Stifel's Peter McGoldrick kept a Hold and said the 12% to 14% operating margin and $3.00 to $3.50 adjusted EPS are above the firm's 11% EBIT margin and $3 EPS view, even though implied revenue is lower than Stifel's about $51.2B (The Fly, Investing.com). RBC kept Sector Perform and a $39 target, called the targets 'more ambitious than expected,' and noted that 12% to 14% margins sit well above a 9.4% consensus and that the EPS range is about 20% above market expectations. RBC also said the path is back-weighted, depends on gross margin recovery and savings, and leaves little room for near-term positive surprises (MarketScreener).

camps.name: Skeptics (Truist, and the late-morning tape)
camps.argues: Truist analyst Joseph Civello said the fiscal 2031 outlook is better than investors expected but 'very back-weighted,' and called it 'aggressive given the current pressures facing the brand itself in a tough time for the category.' He added that management has 'often underestimated pressures in their commentary/plans' (WWD). The fade from a 6.3% gain to a loss of about 2% is this camp's market vote: growth does not return until fiscal 2029, implied fiscal 2031 sales of about $48B are only a little above fiscal 2026, capital returns are dividends only with no buyback commitment, and Sportswear, including Jordan and Converse, is asked to add only about $1B of the $5B increment.

overview.agree: Agree fiscal 2027 is still an investment year (high-single-digit revenue decline, about 6% adjusted operating margin, $1.15 to $1.35 adjusted EPS), that Performance Sports is the intended growth engine, and that the interesting debate is the margin recovery, not a rapid return to mid-teens sales growth.
overview.split: Split on whether 12% to 14% margins and $3.00 to $3.50 of adjusted EPS by fiscal 2031 are a conservative, beatable floor or an aggressive promise from a team that has underestimated pressure, and on how much of the $2.5B Pace savings will actually show up in profit.

shift.note: Monday product showcase and a separate UEFA Champions League match-ball deal starting in the 2027-28 season. Nike showed Tuned Air, new Nike Free and Nike Mind footwear, Vaporfly 5, and Sportswear ideas including Project Ride and Morpho X, with most of it arriving over the coming year (Nike release).

9:00 AM Eastern press release sets the 2031 framework and reaffirms fiscal 2027 guidance. Premarket gain of about 6% to 7%. Public webcast begins 8:30 AM Pacific. By late morning the stock had given the gain back and was down about 2%.

overview.hinges: Whether new product actually sells at full price from late 2027 into 2028, whether Greater China and Sportswear or Jordan stabilize, whether Pace savings fall to the bottom line, and whatever else comes out of the rest of the webcast and Q&A, which were still underway when this was written. The next formal earnings date is estimated for December 17.

tickers.whatHappened: Nike hosted its first investor day since 2017 at the Philip H. Knight Campus in Beaverton. The morning press release, which went out at 9:00 AM Eastern, before the 8:30 AM Pacific webcast, introduced Full Stride Ahead, reaffirmed fiscal 2027 guidance, and set a 2031 framework: about $5B of incremental revenue off a fiscal 2027 base (about $4B from Performance Sports and $1B from Sportswear), operating margins of 12% to 14%, and adjusted EPS of $3.00 to $3.50. Fiscal 2027 is still a high-single-digit revenue decline, adjusted operating margin of about 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35, excluding about $0.15 a share of Pace restructuring expense. Declines are expected to moderate in fiscal 2028, with market-level growth targeted in fiscal 2029 and growth above the market in fiscal 2030 and 2031. Pace is expected to deliver about $2.5B of annualized run-rate savings by fiscal 2031, with about $1.3B of pre-tax implementation charges. Capital returns are about $2.4B of dividends in fiscal 2027 and about $12B of cumulative dividends from fiscal 2027 through 2031, with no separate buyback commitment. Five priority sports (running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor), Sportswear (Nike Sportswear, Jordan and Converse), and 23 priority countries are expected to drive more than 90% of growth through 2031. The CFO speaking today is Dave Denton, not Matt Friend; Denton joined about three months ago. Beyond the release, during the webcast CEO Elliott Hill said the more-than-$330B athletic footwear and apparel industry is expected to keep growing 3% to 4% a year (The Fly). Reuters, with Danielle Kaye reporting from Beaverton, quoted Hill telling investors, 'We have a growing market, more ways to serve athletes and advantages built over decades,' while acknowledging 'we have more work to do on inventory, full-price selling, and profitability.' Hill also said Nike aims to double the number of products developed in under 14 months by the end of fiscal 2031, a target that was not in the press release (Reuters). In a CNBC interview with Sara Eisen, Hill said the work is about 'being closer to the athletes we serve' and that 'what's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective.' Caitlin Clark appeared on stage and Paige Bueckers was in a Nike Zoom intro (posts from accounts covering the event). Q&A and later presentations had not been fully reported by late morning Central time; the webcast is scheduled to run until about 12:00 PM Pacific.
tickers.howReading: Credible discussion was heavier in sell-side notes than on X, where the highest-attention posts were headline accounts marking the premarket pop, the $12B dividend plan, and then the reversal. Jefferies was the most constructive (credible, beatable floor). Stifel and RBC treated the margin and EPS targets as more ambitious than their models but kept Hold or Sector Perform because the recovery is back-weighted and implied revenue is modest. Truist was the clearest skeptic, calling the outlook aggressive and back-weighted. Across those notes, the implied fiscal 2031 revenue of about $48B is only a little above fiscal 2026 revenue of about $46.4B (Investing.com; LSEG has fiscal 2027 consensus around $42.84B, which plus $5B gets to roughly the same place). Standing Wall Street consensus, not all from today, is mixed: TipRanks shows 9 Buys, 18 Holds and 10 Sells among 37 analysts over the past three months, with an average target around $36.47, a bit below the mid-morning price. RBC reiterated Sector Perform at $39 today. Cantor Fitzgerald was Neutral at $38 ahead of the event.

facts.value: About $5B of incremental revenue vs fiscal 2027 ($4B Performance Sports, $1B Sportswear), 12% to 14% operating margins, $3.00 to $3.50 adjusted EPS, and about $12B of cumulative dividends from fiscal 2027 through 2031 (Nike release, November 17)

tickers.controversy: The fight is whether the 12% to 14% margin and $3.00 to $3.50 EPS targets by fiscal 2031 are a conservative floor (Jefferies) or an aggressive, back-weighted promise (Truist), and whether a plan that does not restore growth until fiscal 2029, adds only about $5B of sales off a trough year, and returns cash only through dividends is enough. Coverage of Q&A is still incomplete because the event was still running.
